plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional cutaway of a cylindrical capacitor drawn in perspective, extending from the near end at the lower left toward the far end at the upper right. Two concentric conducting cylinders share a common axis: a narrow inner cylinder whose visible near face is crowded with plus signs, and a much wider outer shell whose surface carries minus signs spaced along its length and around its near rim. In the near end view, short red arrows labeled 'E' radiate outward from the inner cylinder across the annular gap to the inner wall of the outer shell, filling the gap uniformly in every radial direction. An orange dashed cylinder of intermediate radius is drawn between the two conductors, appearing as dashed ellipses at both ends joined by dashed lines running the length of the device; a curved leader from the top labels it 'Gaussian surface'. At the far end three arrows fan out from a point on the axis, labeled 'R1', 'r', and 'R2' in order of increasing length. Nesting the dashed surface between the two conductor radii shows precisely which charge it encloses. The geometry sets up the flux calculation that gives the capacitance of a coaxial pair carrying charges plus Q and minus Q.

elements: inner solid conducting cylinder with positive charge markers ('+') on its surface
outer hollow conducting cylinder (shell) with negative charge markers ('-') on its inner surface
dashed orange cylindrical Gaussian surface
electric field (E) vectors (red arrows) pointing radially outward

radius indication arrows at the far end for R1, r, and R2

interactions.label: Gaussian Radius r
interactions.teaches: Moving the surface changes the enclosed charge and the radial distance, directly demonstrating the 1/r dependence of the electric field in the gap.

interactions.label: Highlight Region
interactions.teaches: Clarifies the three distinct domains: E=0 inside the inner conductor, E>0 in the gap due to enclosed +Q, and E=0 outside due to net zero enclosed charge.

demo_steps.title: Electric field in the gap
demo_steps.narration: When r is between R1 and R2, the Gaussian surface encloses the inner conductor's positive charge. The E-field points radially outward and its magnitude decreases as 1/r.

demo_steps.title: Inside the inner conductor
demo_steps.narration: Shrink r below R1. In a static conductor, excess charge resides entirely on the surface, so the enclosed charge is zero. The electric field inside is therefore zero.

demo_steps.title: Outside the capacitor
demo_steps.narration: Expand r beyond R2. The surface now encloses both +Q and -Q. The net enclosed charge cancels to zero, so the electric field outside the coaxial cable vanishes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cylinders are aligned along the X-axis spanning from x = -3 to x = 3. Inner conductor: R1 = 1.0, rendered as a solid pale grey cylinder. Outer conductor: inner radius R2 = 2.5, outer radius 2.8, rendered as a transparent blue-grey shell (opacity 0.3, #a6b8d4). Gaussian surface: radius r (driven by the slider), rendered with orange dashed lines (#ffa500) forming circular ends and longitudinal connecting lines. Plus signs are distributed over the r = 1.0 surface, minus signs over the r = 2.5 inner surface. E-field red arrows (#e60000) originate at the inner cylinder and point radially outward; their length dynamically scales as 1.5/r when 1.0 < r < 2.5, and they disappear when r < 1.0 or r > 2.5. At x = 3, black arrows originate from the axis indicating R1 and R2, alongside an orange dashed arrow tracking r.
interactionPlan.notes: The region toggle should visually highlight the respective volumetric zone (e.g., by slightly elevating its opacity or desaturating the rest) and can be used to independently set the slider to the representative values defined in the demo steps. Ensure E-field arrows dynamically update length and visibility based on the slider.

authoredContext:
A cylindrical capacitor consists of two concentric, conducting cylinders (the figure). The inner cylinder, of radius R1, may either be a shell or be completely solid. The outer cylinder is a shell of inner radius R2. We assume that the length of each cylinder is l and that the excess charges +Q and −Q reside on the inner and outer cylinders, respectively.

With edge effects ignored, the electrical field between the conductors is directed radially outward from the common axis of the cylinders. Using the Gaussian surface shown in the figure, we have

A cylindrical capacitor consists of two concentric, conducting cylinders. Here, the charge on the outer surface of the inner cylinder is positive (indicated by +) and the charge on the inner surface of the outer cylinder is negative (indicated by −).

Figure shows two concentric cylinders. The inner one, with radius R1 has positive signs on it. The outer one, with radius R2 has negative signs on it. Arrows marked E are shown radiating from the inner one to the outer one. A third cylinder, with radius r, is shown as a dotted line between the two. This is labeled Gaussian surface.
